newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Belgian wine industry eyes brewers' fame.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Belgian wine industry eyes brewers' fame.

text.p: Belgium's budding wine industry is challenging nature and the country's reputation as a mecca for beer lovers to gain a place on the short list of high-quality vintages.

A few minutes' drive from Leuven's imposing Interbrew brewery, which has made Stella Artois beer known the world over, the 10 Hagelandse Wijnbouwers (Hageland Winegrowers) dream of their rapidly growing cottage industry gaining equal fame.
Just over 25 years after the first vines were planted, the Hageland association now produces around 70,000 litres, or 100,000 bottles, a year, according to Daems & Sons, the largest of the vineyards.
Trying to cultivate top quality grapes in one of Europe's wettest countries puts the growers in the lap of the gods.

"To get a good wine here we have to work twice as hard as in France," association chairman Maurice Fol told Reuters. "We have fewer grapes, so we have to take extra precaution against birds, and the wasps are really bad."

But the wine growers look to the future with confidence and point to a glorious past when their predecessors supplied the Burgundian dukes who in the Middle Ages ruled much of what is now northern France, Belgium and parts of the Netherlands.
"We are only at the beginning of the renaissance," said Fol.

The Hageland's wine-making tradition died out in the 16th century and was not revived until 1970 when a few friends, following the advice of the local agricultural college, decided to import suitable vines from Germany.
Ninety nine percent of the wine now made is white, based mainly on the Mueller-Thurgau grape.
"It's very dry and a little fruity," said Simmone Daems, wife of former Belgian Senate member Jos Daems, who co-founded the association in 1969.

By blending in other varieties, such as Ortega, Optima and Siegerrebe, even the most experienced connoisseurs have been fooled into thinking they are drinking a refined wine such as a Sancerre from France's Loire Valley.
"Our intention is to make a really excellent wine. We are not interested in quantity, only in quality," said Fol, a retired moral philosophy lecturer.
His son Frank bottles up to 800 litres a year for sale in his Leuven restaurant.
The Fols attribute the quality of Hageland wine to the area's micro-climate and shallow iron-rich soil.
But they admit things can go wrong.

Their 1993 vintage won a merit award at the 1996 Brussels world wine competition organised by the International Union of Oenologues. But 1994's product was so bad it was left off the Fol restaurant's 300-strong wine list.

The 1995 vintage, due to be bottled in November, should be better, Maurice Fol predicted, but judging 1996 was impossible: the grapes are not due to be picked until around October 15 because of late flowering in June.
The association is applying to the government of the Dutch-speaking region of Flanders for Hageland wine to get a quality label equivalent to the French appellation d'origine controlee (AOC).

If successful the 10 Hageland vineyards would be the first of Belgium's 17 winemakers to receive such an award, according to the Belgian Federation of Wine and Spirit Makers, which is backing their application.
Quality label or not, the reality is that Belgian wines will probably never grace dinner tables outside the country.
"There are 10 million people here. We are producing only 100,000 bottles a year," said Andre Janssens, the Hageland's second largest producer.
Interbrew, at its Leuven factory alone, can produce up to 250,000 bottles of Stella Artois an hour.
"We're not in competition (with Interbrew). Their directors drink our wine and I drink their Stella when I'm thirsty," said Fol. "But wine is not to be drunk, it's to be savoured."
